summary: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) normally needs configuration on both ends. This document describes unsolicited BFD, where one side can start a session and the other creates it automatically, subject to policy. That simplifies "sessionless" applications. It also defines a YANG module to configure and manage the feature.

eli5.summary: Usually two friends must both agree to a check-in game. Here one friend starts it and the other just joins, as long as the house rules say that's fine.

subtitle: Lets one router start a BFD liveness session and the other join automatically, with no per-session setup.

tldr.problem: BFD sessions usually must be configured or registered on both ends. For applications with no natural session between the endpoints, such as static routes or Route Server next hops at an IXP, that coordination is a burden.
tldr.mechanism: One side takes the Active role and starts sending BFD Control packets. The Passive side, if enabled by configuration and policy, creates a matching session when it sees a packet with Your Discriminator 0. A YANG module configures it.
tldr.outcome: A session can be started from one side only, limited to single-hop BFD and guarded by interface, subnet and host policy. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9468 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880 and RFC 5881) usually needs a session to be configured or registered on both sides. That is easy when an application such as BGP already has a session involving both ends. It is harder for "sessionless" applications, where both sides must be configured at the same time even though only one side wants BFD.

This RFC defines unsolicited BFD: a session can be initiated by only one side and established without explicit per-session configuration or registration by the other side, subject to per-interface or global policy. It changes only how sessions are initiated. The Echo function, Demand mode and other procedures of RFC 5880 are unchanged.
sections.eli5: Normally both friends have to sign up for the check-in game. Here only one has to sign up, and the other joins when the first calls.

sections.title: Why Sessionless Applications Need It
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. First, BFD can track the liveness of the next hop of a static route. Only one side may need it, yet both sides must be configured, and sometimes static routes are created just for BFD. Second, BFD can track the third-party next hop of BGP routes learned from a Route Server at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP). That next hop differs from the Route Server peering address, so the two routers would need routes and next hops from each other.

Compared with Seamless BFD (RFC 7880), this approach is a minor procedural enhancement to widely deployed BFD, and it needs no out-of-band exchange of BFD discriminators before bring-up. It applies only to single IP hops. Multihop (RFC 5883) is excluded because of security risks.

With BGP ADD-PATH at an IXP, unsolicited BFD can feed BGP route resolvability so routes whose NEXT_HOP is unreachable are excluded.
sections.eli5: If you only want to know whether your neighbor is home, it is silly to make the neighbor fill in paperwork too. You just knock, and they answer.

sections.title: Active and Passive Procedures
sections.content:
One side takes the Active role and the other the Passive role, as in RFC 5880 Section 6.1. Passive support MUST be disabled by default and MUST need explicit configuration. On the passive side, bfd.DesiredMinTxInterval, bfd.RequiredMinRxInterval and bfd.DetectMult SHOULD be configurable. The passive side MAY instead use the values the active side puts in its packets, but it MUST choose its own bfd.LocalDiscr so that multiple unsolicited sessions can exist.

The active side starts sending BFD Control packets. The passive side sends nothing at first. When it receives a packet with 0 as Your Discriminator and finds no existing session, it SHOULD create a matching session unless configuration or policy forbids it. On a numbered interface, the packet's source address MUST be in the subnet of the receiving interface, or the packet MUST NOT be processed.

The passive side then sends Control packets and runs normal bring-up, maintenance and tear-down. If the session does not come up within an implementation-specific time (at least the local failure detection time), or if an established session goes down, it MUST stop sending and SHOULD delete the session until the active side starts again. It may retain the state for a while for operational purposes.

The RFC adds one state variable, bfd.Role, with values Active or Passive.
sections.eli5: One kid starts waving. The other, if the house rules allow, waves back. If the waving stops working, the second kid stops and waits until the first starts again.

sections.title: The YANG Data Model
sections.content:
The RFC defines the module ietf-bfd-unsolicited, which augments the BFD YANG model of RFC 9314 and follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). Unsolicited parameters for IP single-hop sessions can be set at two levels: globally for all interfaces, and per interface, which needs the unsolicited-params-per-interface feature. When both exist, the per-interface setting wins.

Each level holds a local multiplier and either separate desired-minimum-transmit and required-minimum-receive intervals or a single minimum interval. Each interface also has an enabled flag, false by default. For monitoring, a read-only role leaf is added to each session.
sections.eli5: There is a settings page with house-wide defaults and room-by-room overrides. The room setting wins when both exist.

sections.title: A Configuration Example
sections.content: The RFC shows how to configure the passive end. Globally, the local multiplier is 2 and the minimum interval is 50 ms. Interface eth0 is enabled with a multiplier of 3 and a minimum interval of 250 ms. Interface eth1 is enabled with no parameters, so it inherits the global values.
sections.eli5: The house rule says check every 50 ms. One room asks for a different rule. Another room has no rule of its own, so it follows the house.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main new risk is excessive resource use by BFD from "unexpected" remote systems. Implementations MUST limit the feature to specific interfaces and single-hop sessions using the procedures of RFC 5082, apply policy so BFD packets are processed only from certain subnets or hosts, and deploy it only where anonymous participation is not offered, such as an IXP or a provider-customer link.

Implementations are RECOMMENDED to use BFD authentication, and the strongest supported mechanism MUST be used. At an IXP this may be impossible because the two endpoints are not coordinated, but for static-route next hops it is possible at the cost of configuring matching key chains.

For the YANG module, writable nodes such as enabled and the interval and multiplier settings can affect network operation if written without protection. The RFC points to NETCONF or RESTCONF secure transport and NACM access control.
sections.eli5: Letting anyone start a game with you could wear you out. So you only play with people on your own street, and ideally check their ID.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA registered the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-bfd-unsolicited in the IETF XML Registry and registered the YANG module ietf-bfd-unsolicited, with prefix bfd-unsol, in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: The new settings page got its official name in the public directory.
